$comment: Rendering ceilings for four flows: the Health overview (`/dashboard`), the runs list, run
detail and quarantine. The landing page, Home (`/dashboard/now`), is not measured yet: it
needs a reading on the reference install (plan D18). A **baseline**, not a live observation — `pnpm test:render`
measures a real browser and compares against this.
The shape is the ratchet the repository already uses for coverage and complexity:
a floor is recorded once, deliberately and by hand, and thereafter only a
regression fails. That is what keeps the gate from being turned off — a gate whose
own threshold can be rewritten in the same commit is a gate that agrees with the
tree instead of the code. `render:baseline` is `never-in-ci` in gate-tooling.json
for exactly that reason.
`recorded: false` is a MEASUREMENT phase, not a failing one, and the distinction is
enforced rather than documented. `scripts/lib/render-gate-phase.mjs` derives the tier
`test:render` is allowed to have from this file, and `gate-tooling.test.mjs` fails until
`scripts/gate-tooling.json` agrees. So:
- `recorded: false` -> the CI job measures the four routes, publishes the numbers to
the job summary, compares nothing, and is tiered `pr-reporting` — not a required
check. A required check that can never pass blocks every pull request and teaches
reviewers to ignore red.
- `recorded: true`  -> the same spec compares against these ceilings and fails on a
regression, and `test:render` must be `pr-blocking`. Leaving it below that is a
real gate nobody is required to satisfy, which is the worse state.
Graduating is therefore one commit with two parts: record a real run, and raise the
tier. The test refuses to pass if only one of them happened, so `recorded: true`
beside invented numbers cannot quietly become a gate that is green and unenforced.
Why the budget has to exist before the effect does: `backdrop-filter` repaints the
backdrop on every frame, and the whole of the glass argument is about that cost. The
budget therefore has two halves and they are not the same kind of number:
- `lcpMs`/`inpMs`/`cls`/`longTasks` are TIMINGS. They were recorded on the reference
install on 2026-10-21 and are compared on every pull request.
- `glassStackDepth` is a STRUCTURAL CEILING. It is not a timing and does not depend
on hardware — it is how deeply translucent surfaces nest on that route, which is a
property of the component tree rather than of the data. It is compared in every
phase, because a budget that ships an unmeasured cost is the defect `RF-9`
recorded. Adding glass without it would have been adding compositing
work to four routes under a gate that watches none of it.
**Depth, not a total, and the first run showed why.** Counting every element with a
computed `backdrop-filter` gave 10 on `/dashboard/runs` and 2 on `/dashboard/quarantine`
with one run seeded — the route has one card per row. A ceiling of 10 would have been a
statement about how many runs existed when the budget was written, and the dashboard
would have failed its own budget when a second run landed. Depth cannot grow with a row
count, so it is a constraint the design can hold. Depth is also the closer cost proxy: a
translucent panel samples everything painted behind it, so two stacked panels composite
roughly four times the area of one.
The count is of *elements with a computed `backdrop-filter`*, not of elements carrying
a glass class, so a token that stops applying stops counting.
**The ceiling is 1 on every route since 2026-11-10.** The premium pass makes the chrome
translucent: the sidebar, the phone top bar and bottom tab bar, and the copilot panel frost
the shell glow (`bg-shell`). They sit beside or above the page, never inside it, so depth is 1
and a panel inside a panel is still a failure. Measured before the change: depth 1 over 3
surfaces on all four routes, with LCP 176-220 ms against the 460 ms ceiling, unchanged from
the flat plane. Evidence stays opaque: theme-resolution.test.ts lists every translucent file.
Before that:
**The ceiling is 0 on every route, and still is after 4.0.0.** 4.0.0 admits one translucent
material, `surface-translucent`, on the overlays only: the command palette, dialogs, popovers
and toasts. None of them is open while a route is measured, and a closed dialog is opaque
until it opens (`open:surface-translucent`), because a mounted `<dialog>` reports its
computed backdrop filter even while hidden. So the four routes composite nothing at rest, and
any computed `backdrop-filter` this spec finds is a regression it reports by route. The
depth counter is kept because a rule that nothing measures in a real browser is a rule on paper.
How it is populated: `pnpm render:baseline` on the reference install builds the web
bundle, serves it with `vite preview`, measures each route once, and writes the reading
to `observed` and `ceilingFor(observed)` to the metric keys. **A ceiling is never the
reading itself**: the ceilings are compared on the CI runner, which read the same bundle
about 1.7-2x slower than the reference install on 2026-10-21 (LCP 236-264 ms against
112-152 ms), so `CEILING_RULES` in scripts/lib/rendering-budget.mjs gives LCP and INP 3x
with floors of 460 ms and 150 ms, CLS 2x with a floor of 0.05, and long tasks +2.
The LCP and INP floors were raised from 300/100 to 460/150 on 2026-11-04. For the four
primary routes the reference readings are low enough that `3x` falls under the floor, so
the floor — not the factor — is the binding ceiling on them. The old floors sat below the
CI runner's own clean range: across 23 CI runs `/dashboard` read LCP up to 404 ms and INP
up to 112 ms, so a third of runs failed on the gap between two machines rather than on any
regression. The floors now clear those observed CI maxima with margin. The `observed` block
below is still the 2026-10-21 reference reading; the metric keys are deliberately held at
those floors rather than at `ceilingFor(observed)`, because re-recording captures one noisy
run and bakes its `3x` into the ceiling (a single re-record read LCP 332 on one route and
would have set a 1000 ms ceiling). Review the diff before committing it — the point of
recording the number once is that the next change has to beat it, and a regression that
doubles a heavier route's reading still fails.
reason: Observations recorded by `pnpm render:baseline` on 2026-10-21 on the reference install — a self-hosted single node (Intel Core i7-13650HX, 31.7 GB, Windows 11 Pro), PostgreSQL 16 in Docker, the web bundle under `vite preview`. Each route's `observed` block is that reading. The metric-key ceilings are `ceilingFor(observed)` under the CEILING_RULES floors raised to LCP 460 / INP 150 on 2026-11-04 (see the `$comment` above for why the floor dominates these light routes and why a re-record was not taken). Closes PERF-1, and `test:render` is `pr-blocking`.

/dashboard.$why: The Health overview. It was the first paint a person saw until `/` moved to Home (`/dashboard/now`), which this budget does not measure yet. It replaced /login, which no longer exists (ADR-006). Opaque like everything else, Glass depth 1: the translucent chrome beside the page, never the evidence on it.

/dashboard/runs.$why: The runs list. The heaviest of the four: every row is a run, and a slow one here is a dashboard that appears to hang. Opaque rows on an opaque plane, Glass depth 1: the translucent chrome beside the page, never the evidence on it.

/dashboard/runs/:runId.$why: Where a person decides whether a release is safe, so a rendering defect here is the most expensive one in the product. Evidence is never read through a translucent surface: Glass depth 1: the translucent chrome beside the page, never the evidence on it.

/dashboard/quarantine.$why: The filter surface, and the only primary flow whose content changes on every keystroke — so its INP is the reading most likely to catch an unthrottled re-render. Opaque, Glass depth 1: the translucent chrome beside the page, never the evidence on it.
